title: Investigation on the influence of exergame and VR-based back training on pain reduction and mobility in chronic non-specific back pain
summary:
For years, back pain has led the statistics for reasons for incapacity for work and medical rehabilitation. Low back pain is defined as pain below the costal arch and above the buttock folds, with or without radiation. Chronic low back pain refers to pain episodes that last longer than twelve weeks. Programs that promote muscle strengthening and stabilization (particularly the core muscles) appear to achieve better results in relieving low back pain symptoms than cardiorespiratory programs.
Serious games, i.e. computer games with a serious background, are increasingly being used for therapeutic support in the areas of health promotion, prevention and rehabilitation. It has been described in the literature that so-called gamification elements can contribute to pain reduction in non-specific back pain. In addition to exergame-based therapy applications, the use of head-mounted systems, in which the pain is distracted by displaying virtual reality (VR), proves to be useful in these situations. The study registered here aims to measure the influence of exergame and VR-based physical training compared to physical functional training on pain perception, finger-floor distance, well-being and core strength.

interventions.name: Patients with chronic non-specific back pain who complete eight weeks of functional training using the ICAROS Health Setup
Patients with chronic non-specific back pain who complete eight weeks of functional training in a conventional physiotherapeutic setting

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients aged 18 and over with a medical diagnosis of chronic back pain are included.
Exclusion criteria:
People under the age of 18 are generally excluded. Furthermore, chronic back pain patients with an acute herniated disc, a vertebral fracture or existing osteoporosis are excluded, as well as patients with chronic back pain in whom the back pain is due to inflammation, a tumor or an acute trauma.
